inputs.original_text: President John Mahama says national policy should reflect the law, culture, and collective agreement, and that he is committed to the rule of law as human-rights debates grow more complex. But “collective agreement” and cultural norms can’t be excuses to leave vulnerable people behind. The rule of law matters most when it protects everyone’s rights, including those with the least power to shape the consensus.
inputs.modified_text: John Mahama’s commitment to the rule of law is meaningful only if the law protects people with the least power—not just those whose views dominate a “collective agreement.” Culture and consensus are shaped by inequality, so they cannot be treated as neutral reasons to deny vulnerable people their rights. A fair society must make human rights a limit on majority power, not a prize people receive only when the majority approves.
